summary.text: A chemical bond is an attraction that holds atoms or ions together in molecules, crystals and other structures.
Bonds come as ionic (charged ions attracting), covalent (shared electrons), metallic, or a mix, and they come from how the outer electrons of atoms behave.
Which kind of bond holds a material together decides its structure and properties, such as how strong, soft or brittle it is.

facts.label: Three strong types
facts.value: Covalent, ionic and metallic bonds are the strong, primary bonds

facts.label: Weak bond examples
facts.value: Hydrogen bonds and the London dispersion force are weak, secondary bonds

facts.label: Why ionic crystals crack
facts.value: Forces between ions are short-range, so cracks are not bridged

facts.label: Metal electron sea
facts.value: Each metal atom donates electrons to a shared sea between atoms

facts.label: Network covalent solids
facts.value: Diamond and quartz are covalent bonds extending through a whole solid

items.prompt: You drop a lump of table salt and it shatters instead of bending. What best explains this?

options.label: Its ions attract only at short range, so a crack is not bridged
Its electrons roam freely between all the atoms in the lump
Its bonds are weak and break at the slightest push of force
Its atoms share pairs of electrons along fixed chains in space

items.explain: Ionic bonds are strong but brittle because the forces between ions are short-range and do not bridge cracks.

items.prompt: A blacksmith hammers a bar of metal flat and it does not snap. Which bonding idea explains why?

options.label: Ions locked in place, each attracting only its nearest neighbours
Shared electrons forming a few fixed lines between pairs of atoms
Electrons in a shared sea, with atoms not attracted in set directions
Weak attractions between separate small molecules in the metal

items.explain: Metallic bonding is collective and not oriented in particular directions, so metal crystals deform more easily, which gives malleability.

items.prompt: Candle wax is soft and melts at a low temperature, yet it is built from covalently bonded molecules. Why?

options.label: The covalent bonds inside each molecule are very weak
The forces holding one molecule to the next are much weaker
The molecules are held together by a sea of electrons
The molecules are made of oppositely charged ions

items.explain: Covalent bonds make small molecules, and the weak intermolecular forces between them give waxes and oils their soft bulk and low melting points.

items.prompt: A diamond is far harder and has a much higher melting point than a wax candle. Both rely on covalent bonds. What is the difference?

options.label: Diamond's covalent bonds extend in a network through the whole solid
Diamond is held together by ions of opposite charge instead
Diamond has no bonds between its atoms, only loose contact
Diamond's bonds are weaker but there are simply more of them

items.explain: Covalent bonds that extend in networks through a solid, as in diamond, give strong, tough structures with high melting points, unlike small separate molecules.

items.prompt: A chemist finds a bond that is partly sharing and partly attraction between charges. What should she conclude about the types of bond?

options.label: The sample must be contaminated, since bonds are always one pure type
Only metals can show a mixture like this in practice
The bond must be a weak, secondary bond of some kind
Types of bond merge into each other, with no clear line between them

items.explain: The behaviours of valence electrons merge into each other, so no clear line separates the bond types, though the labels remain useful.

items.prompt: In a simple picture of an ionic bond, what happens to the bonding electron?

options.label: It is passed from one atom to the other, leaving opposite charges
It is shared equally between the two nuclei in the middle
It joins a sea of electrons spread over many atoms
It is lost entirely and no longer affects either atom

items.explain: The electron is transferred, so one atom becomes positive and the other negative, and their electrostatic attraction forms the bond.
